slides.0.title: The WSET Systematic Approach to Tasting (SAT)
slides.0.subtitle: Describe precisely, conclude with evidence
slides.1.title: Appearance and nose
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Appearance
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Clarity, colour intensity and hue (lemon, gold, ruby, garnet, tawny and so on); changes in hue hint at age and oxidation
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Condition and intensity of the nose
slides.1.highlights.1.content: First check for faults (e.g. TCA, excess volatile acidity), then judge intensity and development (youthful, developing, fully developed, tired)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Primary, secondary, tertiary
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Primary: variety and fruit (fruit, floral, herbaceous); secondary: winemaking (lees, buttery MLF, oak); tertiary: ageing (dried fruit, leather, mushroom, nuts). The classification is itself evidence for deduction
slides.1.content: Aroma notes are not just lists of nouns: separating primary, secondary and tertiary lets you deduce winemaking and age.
slides.2.title: Palate and conclusions
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Structure
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Sweetness, acidity, tannin (level and texture), alcohol, body, flavour intensity and finish. Structure is harder for winemaking to disguise than aroma, so it is the backbone for identifying variety and climate
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Quality: BLIC
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Balance, Length, Intensity, Complexity; quality grades run from faulty, poor, acceptable and good to very good and outstanding, each justified with BLIC
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Readiness and identification
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Judge whether it is ready to drink or has ageing potential and say why (acid, tannin, fruit concentration); when identifying variety or region, give at least two or three pieces of structural and aromatic evidence
slides.2.content: The spirit of the SAT: every conclusion can be traced back to the description before it.
slides.3.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Which category does a buttery note belong to?
Diacetyl from MLF is a secondary aroma.
What does the “L” in BLIC stand for?
Short answer: a wine has “intense aromas and a long finish, but acidity is too low and the alcohol burns”. Judge its quality with BLIC and explain.
Balance (B) is poor: low acidity, burning alcohol
A judgement on complexity (C) is needed
Conclusion: good but not very good, or a similar justified grade
Readiness: low acidity limits ageing potential

Intensity and length are positives, but balance is poor: too little acidity and burning alcohol make the wine heavy; if the aromas lack layers, complexity is only moderate. Overall “good”, because the balance flaw keeps it from “very good”. Low acidity also limits ageing potential, so drink now.
